author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow because it explains its terms from first principles (the replication slot as a bookmark, resurrection, the search rule, refresh interval), and it adds a freshness budget table, a failure table with a data-lost column and a section on where progress is kept, while A is just as rigorous but denser and assumes more prior knowledge.

author: sonnet
reason: A is easier for an outsider to learn the system from: its summary is clearer, it defines more of the basics (replication slot, offsets, refresh interval, resurrection) with concrete numbers, its diagram is cleaner, and its failure table says what data is lost in each case, while B packs similar content into denser, more scattered notes.

author: sonnet
reason: B explains the same system and goes further: it has a failure-to-outcome table, gives the batching and gate rules in exact terms, records how S is captured, and includes a concrete rollout that settles the cron cutover A leaves open, all while staying easy to read.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the whole mechanism in its opening paragraph, splits its diagram into clearly labeled live and rebuild paths, and adds a failure table and a concrete rollout, so an outsider can see how the system works more easily than with B's tangled alias diagram and its many undecided items.

author: haiku
reason: A explains how the system works precisely and in full: the outbox row states, retry and batch-error behaviour, cursor movement and how phones apply downloads. B is shorter but contradicts itself ("one row per note" versus a new row for edits made while a change is in flight) and leaves things vague, such as whether a second sync trigger "waits or is dropped".

author: haiku
reason: A explains the whole mechanism (local-first edits, a one-row-per-note outbox, idempotent uploads keyed by change id, a seq-ordered change log with a cursor, conflict notes) in a short, readable form, and it includes the key reason seq order must match commit order; B covers more edge cases and states, but it is much longer, its diagram has a lost-response alt branch, and it contains a confusing slip ("seq 101 is not higher than 6") that mixes up seq and version.

author: haiku
reason: A says where each piece of state lives, defines sent and waiting changes, explains what the phone does with each push result and with each pull entry, and shows how partial failures recover, so a newcomer can build the whole mechanism from it; B is shorter but leaves those same points vague or lists them as open questions.

author: haiku
reason: B says where each piece of state lives and settles points that A leaves open: the base version a waiting change uses, what the phone does with each push result, how a pull inserts a conflict note the phone has never seen, and that syncs never overlap. It also gives a failure outcome for each step, so a newcomer can follow the whole system without guessing.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the system more precisely and completely: where each piece of state lives, the exact retry and in-flight-edit rules, and honest open points. B is looser: it says to "retry with backoff" even though syncs only start on fixed triggers, and it claims "Open questions: None" while leaving gaps such as notes created offline.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives concrete table schemas and spells out the mechanics behind each guarantee, such as the sent flag and next_body for edits made mid-upload and the current note state returned with a conflict, and it lists real open points. A is tidier, but it is vaguer on these edge cases and claims there are no open questions.

author: sonnet
reason: B's worked sequence diagram traces concrete versions, sequence numbers and a lost-reply retry from start to finish, and it adds a rules-and-limits summary, more failure cases (such as the app being killed) and a build order, so an outsider can learn how the system works faster.

author: sonnet
reason: A's sequence diagram walks one concrete case all the way through, with actual version numbers, log sequence numbers, a lost reply and its safe retry, the conflict and how it reaches both phones, so a newcomer can see the whole mechanism in one place; B's diagram is abstract, and its useful extra detail on failures (server errors partway through a batch, a change that blocks the outbox) doesn't make up for that.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to learn from: it starts by explaining what the system is and how it works today, then gives a concrete local schema built on generations, plus test scenarios and risks, while A is more exhaustive but denser and reads like a state machine aimed at someone who already knows the design.

author: haiku
reason: A explains how today's system works before it proposes anything, defines a short set of terms, and builds one clean model (numbered generations, a snapshot, an ordered replay and a one-step swap), so an outsider can follow the design end to end more easily than B, which is more exhaustive but spreads the same ideas across more state fields, platform details and cross-referenced steps.

author: haiku
reason: A is denser, but it defines the whole sync state machine (mode, start_seq, cursor, catch_up_seq, last_seq) and how each state maps to a step, so it closes gaps B leaves open; for example, in B a failed restart after a resync leaves last_seq cleared while download_state may still say complete.

author: haiku
reason: A explains the same two-phase design in plainer terms, defining even Postgres and SQLite and keeping one last_seq, while B's extra state (mode, catch_up_seq, the swap waiting on open reads) makes it more rigorous but harder for a newcomer to follow.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to pick up: its summary explains why the staging copy exists, the rules that apply everywhere are stated once at the top, and the failure table and test list show at a glance how the system behaves, while A is somewhat more rigorous (it has an explicit resync_pending state) but denser to read.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the same watermark, staging and swap design with a simpler state model (one generation column and a three-value staging phase, against B's two tables and seven statuses), plus a failure summary table and concrete tests, so an outsider can build a mental model of the system faster.

author: sonnet
reason: A spells out the full state machine (phase values, which step each trigger resumes at, catchup_seq, empty-response next_seq) and its edge cases precisely, while B leaves resume dispatch and the end-of-download signal vague.

author: sonnet
reason: B is the one I would rather be handed: its explicit `phase` state machine and trigger dispatch, its exact `next_seq` and empty-response semantics, and its coverage of edge cases (a new product with a lower id, a product deleted before its page was fetched, the 1.6 GB disk need, edits that land between catch-up and swap) leave fewer gaps, while A has a dangling reference to a nonexistent "step 7" and never says how the client picks which step to resume.
